title: Curvature-Induced Geometric Universality in Non-Hermitian Anderson Transitions
authors: Chen Wang, Run-Qiu Yang, X. R. Wang, Hechen Ren
abstract: In Euclidean space, universality classes of Anderson transitions are primarily determined by symmetry and spatial dimensionality. Here, we present evidence for a geometry-controlled universality class of non-Hermitian Anderson transitions on hyperbolic-like lattices. In this setting, critical behavior is influenced by the large-scale hyperbolic geometry, characterized by negative curvature, exponential volume growth, and a non-Euclidean notion of spatial scaling. Finite-size scaling of participation ratios across several distinct \( \{p,q\} \) tilings reveals one-parameter scaling collapses with a common critical exponent \( ν\simeq1 \) within numerical accuracy. A complementary phenomenological coarse-grained Landau-Ginzburg analysis shows how exponential correlation-volume growth suppresses critical fluctuations, offering a rationale for the observed mean-field-like scaling. Our results suggest that spatial curvature can act as an additional organizing principle for Anderson-transition universality beyond the conventional dimensionality- and symmetry-based classification.
summary:
This work explores Anderson transitions on negatively curved, hyperbolic lattices, finding that the critical behavior is universal ($
u \simeq 1$) regardless of the specific tiling used. This suggests that the large-scale negative curvature of the geometry itself dictates the universality class, providing a geometric organizing principle beyond traditional symmetry rules.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the critical behavior (universality class) of Anderson transitions in non-Hermitian systems is dictated by the underlying geometry when the lattice is hyperbolic, rather than just symmetry or dimensionality.
main_result:
The critical behavior exhibits a common critical exponent ($
u \simeq 1$) across various hyperbolic tilings, suggesting that the negative curvature of the geometry acts as a universal organizing principle.
method: The analysis combines finite-size scaling of the participation ratio with a complementary phenomenological coarse-grained Landau-Ginzburg field theory approach.
model_or_system: The system is a non-Hermitian Anderson model defined on hyperbolic-like lattices, specifically restricted patches of $\{p, q\}$ tilings. The Hamiltonian is a tight-binding model with complex, disorder-induced hopping and on-site energies.
key_observables:
Critical disorder strength ($W_c$), critical exponent ($
u$), and the disorder-averaged participation ratio ($p_2$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($W$), hyperbolic tiling parameters ($\{p, q\}$), and the effective length scale ($	ilde{L} = \ln N$).
main_assumptions: The critical behavior is assumed to be governed by the large-scale hyperbolic geometry, leading to exponential volume growth that suppresses critical fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures compare wave-function distributions and show finite-size scaling collapses for different hyperbolic tilings, demonstrating consistent critical exponents.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model on hyperbolic lattices, then applies finite-size scaling to determine critical exponents, and finally uses a Landau-Ginzburg analysis to provide a physical rationale for the observed geometric universality.
why_interesting: The concept of geometric universality suggests that fundamental physical properties (like critical exponents) can be determined by the global geometry of the embedding space, offering a powerful new organizing principle beyond standard symmetry classifications.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic comparison of a Euclidean triangular lattice and three representative {p, q} hyperbolic tilings, where each polygon has p sides and q polygons meet at each vertex: (a) the triangular lattice with {p, q} = {3, 6}; (b–d) hyperbolic tilings with {p, q} = {3, 7}, {3, 8}, and {3, 9}, respectively. While the Euclidean lattice is flat, the hyperbolic tilings possess negative curvature and exhibit expo- nential volume growth, N(L) ∼η(p, q)L. Finite-size scaling anal- yses indicate that the non-Hermitian Anderson transitions on these hyperbolic-like lattices share a common critical exponent ν ≃1.

FIG. 3. (a) Volume-growth dimension dvol of the {3, q} hyperbolic- like lattices as a function of graph distance L from the center. The slopes of these curves determine the volume-growth factors η(3, q). (b) Critical exponent ν for the {3, q} tilings, which is consistent with ν = 1 (red dashed line) within numerical uncertainty.
